newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary Postabank aid bolsters sector.
newsitem.headline: Hungary Postabank aid bolsters sector.

text.p: The Hungarian government's decision to grant a 12 billion forints ($66.3 million) loan guarantee to Postabank underscores the bank's own weakness and Hungary's determination to support the banking sector, analysts said.

"I was surprised because this kind of guarantee would normally be the task of the owners and not of the Hungarian government," Eva Varhegyi, analyst for Financial Research Kft in Budapest, told Reuters on Friday.

"But the problem with Postabank is that its own capital or equity capital is rather low concerning the balance sheet total. So this guarantee on doubtful loans reduces the necessity of forming loan-loss provisions...(allowing) the bank's own capital to rise."
The loan guarantee, announced after a cabinet meeting on Thursday, came two months after a panic run by depositors who withdrew 24 billion forints from Postabank over four days.

The bank, Hungary's second biggest, is about 35 percent owned by Hungary's social security funds while Austria's Oesterreischische Postsparkasse holds 10.4 percent and Bank Austria has about three percent.

The government said at the time of the February panic that the bank was sound, but shortly afterwards it entirely exempted Postabank from obligatory national bank reserves through April 15 and granted a 50 percent exemption through June 30.

"I know that when there was the depositors' run, the bank (Postabank) later came out saying that they would not require state assistance," said Agatha Pontiki, an analyst with Thomson Bankwatch in Cyprus.
"Then that argument changed down the line and they went into talks with the government about whether they would receive a subordinated loan. Clearly their solvency was weak."
Dealers in Hungary's overnight and forex markets say that Postabank, formerly one of the biggest players, has cut its activity to a minimum, while other banks have set limits on loans to Postabank.
Analysts said there were other "red flags" about Postabank, which grew 44 percent last year at a time when the Hungarian banking sector grew only 20 percent.
The analysts said Postabank just barely met the capital adequacy ratio, which is set at a minimum of eight percent.

The bank also is the only one of Hungary's big banks that is not publicly audited by one of the big six international auditing firms, analysts said. An audit was conducted by Arthur Andersen, one analyst said, but it has not been released.
Postabank officials did not return calls seeking comment.

The loan guarantee was reminiscent of the government's decision in 1995 to pump 12 billion forints into Budapest Bank after Credit Suisse pulled out of a privatisation deal and before General Electric Capital purchased it for about 12 billion forints, analysts said.
But it also showed Hungary's determination to shore up its banking sector at a time when several privatisation deals are pending, analysts said.
The government plans to sell at least a 25 percent stake in Kereskedelmi es Hitelbank and also is hoping that a strategic investor may be found for Postabank.

Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told reporters after the weekly cabinet meeting: "The state is not taking a direct role in the bank (Postabank)... but the government provides the background so that those who want to participate in raising the bank's capital will find it attractive for them".
He added that there had been expressions of interest from two countries in investing in Postabank, but did not identify them.
Political analyst Attila Ledenyi said it was no surprise that the government had decided to help Postabank, whose chairman, Gabor Prinz, is a familiar figure in political circles.

"The government was afraid that if Postabank got into a major crisis it would be bad for the image of banking in Hungary," Ledenyi said. "This explains all the effort that has been made to keep Postabank in shape." ($ = 180.8 Hungarian Forints)
